foods.name: Potato
foods.form: boiled, ripe (flesh of a potato boiled in its skin, no salt; not green)
foods.tagline: Mostly water, mostly carbs, entirely unthreatening. Bring a wheelbarrow.
overview: A boiled ripe potato is about 76.98% water and 1.8 g fibre, with 379 mg potassium and 13 mg vitamin C per 100 g (USDA). It's the backbone of mash, potato salad and any chip-based argument.
The limiting ingredient is the water. At the lab figure you'd need 8.2 kg of boiled potato, about 60 spuds. Potassium is the runner-up at roughly 25.2 kg.

facts.label: Not to be confused with
facts.value: Green or sprouting potatoes (solanine), which this page does not cover

foods.funFact: In 1995 potato plants were grown on the Space Shuttle Columbia in a NASA and University of Wisconsin experiment, making the potato the first vegetable grown in space.

foods.name: Sweet potato (kumara)
foods.form: baked in skin, flesh only, no salt
foods.tagline: Kumara: sweet, orange, and defeated by its own water content.
overview: Baked kumara flesh is about 75.78% water, with 475 mg potassium, 6.48 g sugars and 19.6 mg vitamin C per 100 g (USDA). It also carries a lot of beta-carotene, which is where the orange comes from.
Water wins again: about 8.3 kg of baked kumara, or 46 large ones. Potassium (20.1 kg) and sugars (27.9 kg) trail behind.
foods.funFact: Kumara was brought to Aotearoa by early Polynesian voyagers, centuries before European ships turned up.

foods.name: Carrot
foods.tagline: Good for your eyes. Terrible odds if you're after a lethal dose.
overview: A raw carrot is about 88.29% water, with 320 mg potassium, 69 mg sodium and 4.74 g sugars per 100 g (USDA). The orange is beta-carotene, which your body turns into vitamin A as needed.
The lab-derived limit is the water again: about 7.1 kg of raw carrot, or 120 medium carrots. Rabbits would be insulted on your behalf.
foods.funFact: Early cultivated carrots were purple or yellow; orange ones only became common in Europe around the 1600s.

foods.name: Onion
foods.tagline: It makes you cry before it gets anywhere near making you ill.
overview: A raw onion is about 89.11% water, with 4.24 g sugars, 146 mg potassium and just 4 mg sodium per 100 g (USDA). Most of the sting comes from sulphur compounds released when you cut it.
Working it out gives about 7.1 kg of raw onion, the water again, or 64 medium onions. You would be crying for entirely different reasons by onion number three.

facts.label: The sting
facts.value: Sulphur compounds released when you cut it

foods.funFact: The tears come from syn-propanethial S-oxide, a gas formed when cutting the onion lets an enzyme (lachrymatory factor synthase) get to work on sulphur compounds.

foods.name: Garlic
foods.tagline: You'd be ostracised long before you'd be in any toxicological danger.
overview: Raw garlic is about 58.58% water, with 401 mg potassium, 31.2 mg vitamin C and 17 mg sodium per 100 g (USDA). It has less water than most vegetables, which is why it takes longer to 'get you'.
The water-based limit is about 10.8 kg of raw garlic, roughly 3,600 cloves. Social death arrives at about clove three.

facts.label: Energy
facts.value: 149 kcal per 100 g (high for a vegetable)

foods.funFact: Garlic's smell comes from allicin, which isn't there in a whole clove: it forms when the clove is crushed or chopped and two stored compounds meet.

foods.name: Broccoli
foods.tagline: Eats like a tree, tastes like a lecture. The lethal part is simply water.
overview: Raw broccoli is about 89.3% water, with 89.2 mg vitamin C, 316 mg potassium and 33 mg sodium per 100 g (USDA). It's one of the better vitamin C sources in the veg aisle.
Vitamin C is no threat (about 933.9 kg to reach its lab limit); the water does it first at about 7.1 kg, or 12 whole bunches.
foods.funFact: Broccoli, cabbage, cauliflower, kale and Brussels sprouts are all one species, Brassica oleracea, bred into different shapes.

foods.name: Iceberg lettuce
foods.tagline: 96% water. Which is, awkwardly, the exact thing the maths blames.
overview: Iceberg lettuce is about 95.64% water, with 141 mg potassium and 10 mg sodium per 100 g (USDA). That is the highest water share of the 20 vegetables researched here.
That makes it the quickest route to the water limit: about 6.6 kg of lettuce, or 12 medium heads. In practice you'd be a rabbit by head two.
foods.funFact: Iceberg lettuce is about 95.6% water by weight (USDA), and its crunch is mostly turgor: water-filled cells pushing against their walls.

foods.name: Cucumber
foods.tagline: Cool as one. Technically a fruit, and mostly just very wet.
overview: Cucumber with peel is about 95.23% water, with 147 mg potassium and only 2 mg sodium per 100 g (USDA). There's barely anything to it, which is the whole refreshing point.
The lab limit is the water: about 6.6 kg of cucumber, or 22 whole ones. It would be a very long and very moist salad.

facts.label: Botanically
facts.value: A fruit (a type of berry called a pepo)

foods.funFact: Botanically a cucumber is a fruit, specifically a berry type called a pepo, even though everyone treats it as a salad vegetable.

foods.name: Red capsicum
foods.tagline: Packed with vitamin C. Water still wins the lethality race. Hilarious.
overview: Raw red capsicum is about 92.21% water, with 127.7 mg vitamin C, 4.2 g sugars and 211 mg potassium per 100 g (USDA). Gram for gram that's well over twice an orange's vitamin C (53.2 mg per 100 g, USDA).
Vitamin C would take about 652.3 kg of capsicum to reach its lab limit, so it's the water at about 6.8 kg, or 57 medium capsicums, that's technically in charge.

facts.label: Sweetness
facts.value: Red ones are just ripe green ones, so they're sweeter

foods.funFact: Green, yellow, orange and red capsicums are largely the same plant at different stages: green ones are picked unripe, and red is what it looks like when it's fully ripe.

foods.name: White button mushroom
foods.tagline: Fungi, not veg. Also mostly water, which is the whole punchline.
overview: White button mushrooms are about 92.45% water, with 318 mg potassium, 5 mg sodium and 9.3 µg selenium per 100 g (USDA). They're a fungus, which is why they don't behave like vegetables.
The water gives the answer: about 6.8 kg, or 380 medium mushrooms. At that point you'd be a very full pizza topping.
foods.funFact: White button, cremini and portobello mushrooms are all the same species, Agaricus bisporus, just different strains or stages of maturity.

Water takes the lead at about 8.6 kg, or 83 medium ears. Your dental floss would not survive.
foods.funFact: An ear of corn usually has an even number of kernel rows, commonly 16.

foods.name: Green peas
foods.tagline: The one vegetable everyone actually eats. Lethal mass: absurdly large.
overview: Boiled green peas are about 77.87% water, with 5.93 g sugars, 271 mg potassium and 14.2 mg vitamin C per 100 g (USDA).
The water limit works out at about 8.1 kg, or 51 cups of peas, with sugars at 30.5 kg as the nearest runner-up.

facts.label: Fibre
facts.value: 5.5 g per 100 g, the highest of the 20 vegetables researched here (USDA)

foods.funFact: Gregor Mendel worked out the basic rules of genetic inheritance in the 1850s and 60s by crossing pea plants in a monastery garden.

flagged.name: Spinach (raw)
flagged.reason: attainability: plausible (headline lethal mass under 2,000 g on the conservative oxalate calculation)
flagged.details: Headline = oxalate. Raw spinach has 970 mg oxalate/100 g on average (range 320 to 1,260; Noonan & Savage 1999, Table 1). Oxalic acid has a rat oral LD50 of 375 mg/kg (Fisher SDS, listed for both the dihydrate and the anhydrous acid). Taking 375 mg/kg as the dihydrate gives 261.8 mg oxalate/kg, so lethalFoodGramsAt70kg = 1889 g. On the anhydrous basis it would be 2646 g (would be 'large'); at the top of the oxalate range it's about 1454 g, at the bottom 5727 g. Next-lowest constituent is water at 6893 g. Real-world: only about 2 to 12% of dietary oxalate is absorbed, but the same review notes that 600 g of spinach in one sitting pushed urinary oxalate above the normal range. Not a lethal-dose joke for this site: excluded per the attainability rule. problems: Source access: no web search worked and the USDA FDC API DEMO_KEY was rate-limited (HTTP 429, retry after ~90 min), so composition values were read from the official FoodData Central SR Legacy bulk CSV (April 2018 release, records dated 2019-04-01) at https://fdc.nal.usda.gov/fdc-datasets/FoodData_Central_sr_legacy_food_csv_2018-04.zip. The compositionSource.url is that download; the individual food pages at fdc.nal.usda.gov/food-details/<id>/nutrients are a single-page app that I could not verify by fetch, and 'id' is the SR Legacy FDC ID.

Potato swap: SR Legacy has no 'boiled, flesh and skin' potato. I used 170438 'Potatoes, boiled, cooked in skin, flesh, without salt' (flesh only). The skin is a small share of the weight and is eaten, but it was not blended in because I would have had to invent a ratio.

Forms: sweet potato = baked in skin, flesh (168483); pumpkin = US pumpkin, boiled (168449), not NZ crown or butternut; beetroot = boiled, drained, no salt (169146); sweetcorn = boiled kernels, no salt (169999); peas = boiled, no salt (170420); capsicum = sweet red raw (170108); cucumber = with peel (168409); zucchini = includes skin (169291). Kumara (NZ) varieties differ from the US sweet potato.

Headline is water for 18 of 19 listed foods (lethal masses 6.6 to 10.8 kg). That is a direct consequence of using water's rat LD50, which is only a limit value ('> 90 mL/kg', Fisher/Ricca SDS), not a measured median. Every lethal mass derived from water is therefore a floor, and it's essentially 'the lab limit divided by the water fraction'. PubChem lists no rat oral value for water, only mouse intraperitoneal figures (not used).

Oxalic acid: Fisher lists 375 mg/kg (rat, oral) for BOTH the dihydrate (A219500) and the anhydrous acid (AC186432500). I took the dihydrate basis (oxalate = 69.8% by mass, 261.8 mg oxalate/kg) because it is the conservative one. On the anhydrous basis the oxalate dose is higher and raw spinach would land at about 2646 g (class 'large'), so spinach sits on a classification boundary: the lead may want to override the flag. I did not find a primary rat study for oxalic acid, only the SDS figure; PubChem has a LDLo (600 mg/kg, species unstated) and a dog LDLo (1,000 mg/kg).

Beetroot oxalate: the cited number (275 mg/100 g, range 121 to 450) is for RAW red beetroot (Noonan & Savage 1999, Table 1) and was applied to the boiled form as a conservative upper bound. The OHF food list (https://ohf.org/wp-content/uploads/2024/02/Oxalate-List-022724.pdf) gives 57 mg/100 g for boiled beets but cites no primary sources, so it is not used as the working figure. With 57 the headline would revert to water.

Other oxalate sensitivity check (OHF per-100 g figures, uncited, not used as data): at the working oxalate dose none would beat water: sweet potato (baked/boiled, OHF 126 mg/100 g): 14546 g; potato (boiled, OHF 23 mg/100 g): 79686 g; kale (raw, OHF 10 mg/100 g): 183278 g; carrot (raw, OHF 24 mg/100 g): 76366 g; celery (raw, OHF 25 mg/100 g): 73311 g. Oxalate was therefore not added to those foods.

Potassium: rat oral LD50 comes from one SDS (Fisher, 2,600 mg/kg). PubChem lists guinea pig 2,500 mg/kg and mouse 383 mg/kg oral for KCl; mouse is much lower but a rat value exists, so it's recorded under otherValuesSeen and not used.
Sodium: used PubChem's rat oral 3,000 mg/kg for NaCl; the Fisher SDS says 3,550 mg/kg. Lowest credible value used.

Sugars: 'Sugars, Total' mixes glucose, fructose and sucrose; no rat oral LD50 was found for fructose, so glucose (25,800 mg/kg; sucrose is 29,700) is used as a stand-in. The values never drive a headline.

Not evaluated (no composition figure from FDC and no time to source one): potato glycoalkaloids, nitrate (spinach, beetroot, lettuce), allicin and sulphur compounds (garlic, onion), cucurbitacins (cucumber, zucchini), beta-carotene (high LD50, never limiting), calcium, magnesium and iron (all far above water). Green or sprouted potatoes were excluded by the form given, not tested.
Meta: count is 19 (foods listed); spinach is the 20th assigned food and lives in 'flagged'. Serving units come from FDC portion weights; the 1 kg units are plain arithmetic and have no URL.
Confidence is 'medium' across the board on purpose: composition is high-quality USDA data, but the headline derives from a limit-value LD50 for water.
